passage:
"Bro, scene set hai? Canteen at one, full vibe," Preeti said, dropping her bag on the bench.
Pradeep grinned. "Set. But mujhe first ye batao, kal ka match dekha? Total paisa vasool."
"Dekha! That last over, arre, pure heart attack."
Their new classmate Jaya, sitting alone, frowned. "Paisa vasool... is there an English for it?"
Preeti stopped. "Honestly? No. That's why we say it in Hindi. 'Value for money' is too flat."
"And 'timepass'?"
"Same thing. English can't do it."
Jaya laughed. "Okay, I want to learn these. Teach me?"
"Deal," said Pradeep. "Lesson one: 'jugaad'."

qa.q: Where and when did Preeti tell Pradeep to meet?
qa.a: Preeti told Pradeep to meet at the canteen at one.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when Jaya asked whether there is an English word for "paisa vasool"?
qa.a: Preeti felt thoughtful and a little proud. Stopping to say that English is too flat for it shows that the mix is a real way to say things one language alone cannot.

qa.q: What did Pradeep and Preeti do after Jaya asked about the words, and why did it help?
qa.a: They offered to teach Jaya the words, starting with "jugaad". That turned the mixed talk from a private code into something Jaya could join.

qa.q: What might it be like for Jaya, a new classmate, to hear this mixed talk at first?
qa.a: Jaya might feel a little left out, sitting alone and frowning at the words. Asking and being invited to learn them made Jaya feel included.

grounding: A teenager peppers speech with English phrases and Hindi slang to belong to peers, and uses the mix for words a single language lacks.

passage:
I'm Mridul, and my school gang talks in a mash-up that nobody planned. "Yaar, that test was so brutal, sab kuch out of syllabus tha!" I say, and the others nod. If I said it in only English or only Hindi, it would sound like someone else.
My cousin Rashmi Didi noticed at a wedding. "You go all English when you're showing off and all Hindi when you're excited," she said, laughing. I was embarrassed, then curious.
Now I catch myself. Some things need "yaar". Some need "actually". I like that my mixed talk marks my friends and me, and also that it stretches when a single word is too small.

qa.q: Who noticed Mridul's mixed speech at a wedding?
qa.a: Mridul's cousin Rashmi Didi noticed it at a wedding.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when Rashmi Didi described the switching?
qa.a: Mridul felt embarrassed at first and then curious. Being teased kindly made Mridul start noticing when and why the words changed.

qa.q: What did Mridul start doing after the wedding, and what does it show?
qa.a: Mridul began catching the switches and noticing which words fit which feeling. It shows the mixed talk is a choice that carries belonging and meaning.

qa.q: How might Rashmi Didi see Mridul's mash-up?
qa.a: Rashmi Didi sees it with amusement and warmth, since the remark came with laughter. Rashmi Didi notices the pattern in the switching without treating it as a fault.

grounding: A teenager mixes English phrases and Hindi slang to belong to a peer group and to say things one language lacks.

passage:
First week. Zubin had moved from a quiet Parsi colony in Mumbai to a Delhi school, and at lunch his new classmates talked in a fast, mixed stream: "Bro, scene kya hai?" "Full bakwaas test tha." Zubin answered in careful English and felt like a teacher at the wrong table.
Second week. He tried it. "Scene is... chill?" Suraj laughed, not unkindly. "Almost, yaar. Say 'scene sorted hai'." Zubin practised it on the bus home under his breath.
Fifth week. After the basketball trials, Suraj asked how he felt about being picked as reserve. Zubin opened his mouth for the English word and couldn't find one that fit. "Not sad, exactly. Bas... thoda khalipan." Suraj nodded slowly. "Haan. That's exactly it."
That evening, on the group chat, someone typed "Zubin bhai full desi ho gaya" and Zubin grinned at his phone.

qa.q: What did Suraj teach Zubin to say?
qa.a: Suraj taught him to say "scene sorted hai".

qa.q: How did Zubin feel in the first week at lunch?
qa.a: Zubin felt out of place and awkward, answering in careful English like a teacher at the wrong table while everyone else spoke fast mixed talk.

qa.q: What helped Zubin find his way into the group's talk?
qa.a: Practising small phrases with a friendly guide like Suraj, and using mixed words when English alone could not name what he felt.

qa.q: How does Suraj see Zubin's new way of talking?
qa.a: Suraj is warm and encouraging, correcting gently and nodding when "khalipan" names exactly the feeling Zubin meant.

grounding: A teenager learns to mix Hindi and English to belong, and finds the mix names a feeling one language alone lacks.

passage:
"Kiran, you think you invented this 'bro, I'm so done yaar' way of talking? Let your Chandrika Dadi tell you.
"When I was fifteen, in Lucknow, our college crowd thought Hindi alone was for aunties and English alone was for teachers. So we mixed. 'Too much ho gaya.' 'Timepass kar rahe hain.' 'Don't be such a lallu.' My mother would shake her head at the dinner table.
"But one day my best friend Nargis lost her father. At the condolence, I wanted to tell her how I felt and English gave me 'sorry', and Hindi gave me 'dukh'. Neither was enough. I held her hand and said, 'Nargis, I'm here. Tu akeli nahi hai.'
"She told me years later that line stayed with her. Half one language, half the other. That was just how we spoke when we meant it most.

qa.q: Which city did Chandrika Dadi live in at fifteen?
qa.a: She lived in Lucknow.

qa.q: What was young Chandrika feeling when she couldn't find the right word for Nargis?
qa.a: Young Chandrika felt helpless and full of sorrow for her friend, finding that neither "sorry" nor "dukh" was enough.

qa.q: What choice at the condolence mattered, and why?
qa.a: Young Chandrika held Nargis's hand and spoke in mixed Hindi and English, which let her say what one language alone could not.

qa.q: How did Nargis experience Chandrika's words?
qa.a: Nargis felt comforted and less alone, and the mixed line stayed with her for years.

grounding: An elder recalls mixing English and Hindi as a teen to belong, and how the mix expressed what one language lacked.

passage:
Rain had stopped the under-sixteen match at the Nashik ground, and the team crowded under the pavilion's tin roof, dripping and bored. Darshan, the newest player, kept to the edge.
The captain, Yash, was holding court. "Bro, this rain is full timepass. Umpire bhi ekdum confused hai."
The others laughed and answered the same way. Darshan, who spoke only Marathi at home and textbook English at school, tried to join. "The umpire is... very tension-mein?"
A pause. Then Yash slapped his back. "Tension-mein! Perfect, bro."
By the time the rain slowed, Darshan was trading lines with them. When Yash asked how he felt about batting at number seven, Darshan said, "Ekdum mast. But also thoda dar lag raha. Not scared, just... butterflies-wala dar." Yash nodded. "Same, yaar. Every match."
The umpire called them back, and they ran out together.

qa.q: Where did the team crowd while it rained?
qa.a: They crowded under the pavilion's tin roof.

qa.q: What was Darshan feeling before he tried to join in?
qa.a: Darshan felt shy and left out, keeping to the edge as the newest player who spoke Marathi at home and textbook English at school.

qa.q: What helped Darshan feel part of the team?
qa.a: He took a risk by trying the team's mixed way of talking, and Yash welcomed his attempt with a slap on the back instead of correcting him.

qa.q: How does Yash see Darshan's mixed words?
qa.a: Yash finds them fitting and warm, and admits to the same nervous butterflies before every match.

grounding: A teenager uses Hindi, English and slang to belong to teammates, and the mix names a feeling one language alone lacks.

passage: Squeezed against the door of the Janakpuri metro, Ritu and Deepika were replaying the inter-school fest. "Bro, the dance round was literally next level," Ritu said. "Sab log full hype mein the." Deepika laughed. "And your speech? Ekdum solid. Lowkey I got goosebumps." An aunty beside them frowned, trying to follow. At home, Ritu's Papa asked how the fest went, and Ritu said, "Accha tha, Papa," then stopped. How to say the rest? That she had been scared, then the hall cheered, and for a second she felt she belonged on that stage? In Hindi it sounded too heavy, in English too flat. "It was... like, dil se wala feeling," she finally said. Papa smiled. "Samajh gaya." Later she texted Deepika: "today was such a vibe yaar, bas dil khush ho gaya 😊"

qa.q: Where were Ritu and Deepika replaying the fest?
qa.a: Squeezed against the door of the Janakpuri metro.

qa.q: Why did Ritu stop after "Accha tha, Papa"?
qa.a: Ritu felt proud and moved about the stage moment but unsure how to say it; Hindi felt too heavy and English too flat for that feeling.

qa.q: How could Ritu keep her mixed talk and still include listeners like Papa?
qa.a: Keep the words that carry the feeling, like "dil se wala", and add a plain line in the listener's language when they might not follow.

qa.q: What was the metro ride like for the aunty beside them?
qa.a: The aunty seemed puzzled and a little outside the talk, since the mix of slang marked Ritu and Deepika's own group.

grounding: Shows a teenager mixing English phrases and Hindi slang to belong with a peer, and also using the mix to say something neither language alone could.
